1Abstract

PhishGuard AI is an explainable machine-learning cybersecurity application designed to detect phishing websites. Using the UCI Phishing Websites dataset (11,055 records, 30 features), the system trains and compares two supervised classifiers — Logistic Regression and Random Forest — and presents evaluation metrics, feature importance charts, and per-record prediction explanations through an interactive Streamlit dashboard.

11,055website records
30features
93.93%Random Forest accuracy
0.9402Random Forest F1-score

Random Forest achieved a test F1-score of 0.9402 and an accuracy of 93.93%, outperforming Logistic Regression (F1 = 0.9174, accuracy = 91.54%). The application emphasises explainability and responsible use, clearly stating that predictions are probabilistic and should not be used as the sole security mechanism.

2Introduction

Phishing attacks are one of the most prevalent and damaging forms of cybercrime. Attackers create fraudulent websites that mimic legitimate services to steal credentials, financial data, and personal information. According to the Anti-Phishing Working Group (APWG), hundreds of thousands of unique phishing sites are reported every month. Traditional rule-based detection systems struggle to keep pace with the evolving tactics used by attackers, motivating the use of machine learning techniques that can learn from patterns in historical data.

PhishGuard AI addresses this problem by combining classical machine learning with explainable AI (XAI) techniques, enabling both accurate detection and interpretable results. The project is designed to be educational, demonstrating best practices in data science, model evaluation, and responsible AI deployment.

3Problem Statement

The core problem is the automatic, reliable identification of phishing websites from their structural and behavioural features. Naive approaches that rely on blacklists are reactive and miss newly created phishing sites. Machine learning models can detect previously unseen phishing sites by generalising from patterns in known data.

The challenge

A model that simply outputs a 'phishing' or 'legitimate' label provides no insight into why a particular site was flagged, making it difficult for security analysts to validate or act on the decision. This project addresses both the detection and the explainability challenges.

4Objectives

The objectives of PhishGuard AI are:

  1. Load, validate, and explore the UCI Phishing Websites dataset.
  2. Preprocess data, handle missing values, and prevent data leakage.
  3. Train and compare Logistic Regression and Random Forest classifiers.
  4. Evaluate models using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and confusion matrices.
  5. Provide global feature importance explanations (Random Forest built-in and permutation importance).
  6. Deliver per-record prediction explanations identifying the top contributing features.
  7. Present all results through a professional interactive Streamlit dashboard.
  8. Document limitations and responsible-use guidelines clearly.

5Proposed System

PhishGuard AI is a single-file Python application (app.py) built on Streamlit. It encompasses the full machine-learning pipeline: data ingestion, preprocessing, model training, evaluation, explainability, and interactive prediction. The system uses Streamlit's caching decorators to avoid retraining models on every user interaction, making the dashboard responsive.

All functionality is contained in app.py in accordance with the project requirements — no separate training scripts or utility files are used.

6Dataset Description and Source

Dataset
UCI Machine Learning Repository — Phishing Websites (ID 327)
URL
https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/327/phishing
License
Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0)
Citation
Mohammad, R. M., Thabtah, F., & McCluskey, L. (2014). Predicting phishing websites based on self-structuring neural network. Neural Computing and Applications, 25(2), 443–458.

The dataset contains 11,055 website records. Each record has 30 pre-extracted features covering three families of indicators:

  • URL characteristics — e.g. presence of IP address, URL length, use of shortening services.
  • SSL and domain properties — e.g. SSL certificate state, domain age, DNS record.
  • Page-level indicators — e.g. iframe usage, right-click disabling, form handler destination.

The original target label uses three classes: -1 (phishing), 0 (suspicious), 1 (legitimate). In this project, classes -1 and 0 are mapped to binary label 1 (phishing) and class 1 is mapped to 0 (legitimate), yielding 6,157 legitimate and 4,898 phishing records. No raw URLs are present in the dataset; all features are pre-encoded as integer values (-1, 0, or 1).

7System Architecture

The application follows a linear pipeline architecture within a single Python file, organised into six layers:

Data Layer
load_dataset() reads phishing.csv, normalises column names, maps labels, and validates features.
Preprocessing Layer
preprocess() fills missing values with column medians, removes duplicates, and performs a stratified 80/20 train/test split (random_state=42).
Modelling Layer
train_models() builds two Scikit-learn Pipelines — Logistic Regression (with StandardScaler) and Random Forest (200 trees, class_weight=balanced). Results are cached with @st.cache_resource.
Evaluation Layer
evaluate_model() computes accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and confusion matrix on the held-out test set.
Explainability Layer
compute_rf_feature_importance() uses built-in Random Forest Gini importance; compute_permutation_importance() uses sklearn permutation importance for Logistic Regression.
Presentation Layer
Five Streamlit tabs (Dataset Analysis, Model Evaluation, Explainable AI, Record Analysis, About) render all results interactively.

8Methodology

The project follows the CRISP-DM methodology: Business Understanding, Data Understanding, Data Preparation, Modelling, Evaluation, and Deployment.

  • Business goal: phishing detection with maximum recall on the phishing class.
  • Data understanding: EDA of class distribution, missing values, and feature statistics.
  • Data preparation: imputation and stratified splitting.
  • Modelling & evaluation: two models trained and compared on multiple metrics, with F1-score as the primary selection criterion.
  • Deployment: the final model (Random Forest) is deployed in the Streamlit dashboard.

9Data Preprocessing

Preprocessing steps implemented in app.py:

  1. Column normalisation: all column names converted to lowercase for compatibility with ucimlrepo output.
  2. Label mapping: original UCI labels (-1=phishing, 1=legitimate) mapped to binary (1=phishing, 0=legitimate).
  3. Missing-value imputation: column-wise median imputation for any NaN values in feature columns.
  4. Duplicate removal: exact duplicate rows dropped before splitting.
  5. Stratified train/test split: 80% training, 20% test, stratified by label, random_state=42 for reproducibility.
  6. Feature scaling: StandardScaler applied within each Pipeline to prevent data leakage (scaler fitted on training data only, applied to test data).

10Machine Learning Algorithms

Logistic Regression

Logistic Regression is a linear probabilistic classifier. It estimates the probability that a sample belongs to the positive class (phishing) using the logistic sigmoid function. Its advantage is interpretability through coefficient magnitudes.

Parameters: max_iter=1000, class_weight=balanced, random_state=42, with StandardScaler preprocessing.

Random Forest Classifier

Random Forest is an ensemble of 200 decision trees built with bootstrap sampling. Each tree sees a random subset of features at each split, reducing variance and correlation between trees. It generally achieves higher accuracy than linear models on structured tabular data.

Parameters: n_estimators=200, class_weight=balanced, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1 (parallel training).

Why accuracy alone is insufficient

In an imbalanced or critical detection scenario, a model predicting all samples as 'legitimate' on a 55/45 split achieves 55% accuracy but misses all phishing sites. F1-score balances precision and recall. For phishing detection, Recall (sensitivity) on the phishing class is especially important because a False Negative (missed phishing site) is far more dangerous than a False Positive (flagging a safe site).

11Explainable AI Approach

Two explainability methods are implemented:

  1. Random Forest built-in feature importance (Gini importance): measures the mean decrease in node impurity across all trees for each feature. Efficient and built-in, but biased towards high-cardinality features.
  2. Permutation importance (sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance): measures the drop in F1-score when each feature's values are randomly shuffled. Averaged over 10 repeats. More reliable as a model-agnostic measure and used for Logistic Regression.

For per-record explanations, the top 10 globally important features are extracted and their values are highlighted as suspicious (value = -1) or normal (value = 1/0).

Note

This is an approximation based on global importance — not a true per-instance SHAP explanation. This limitation is clearly stated in the dashboard.

12Implementation Details

All code resides in app.py (approximately 600 lines). Key implementation decisions:

  • @st.cache_data used for load_dataset and preprocess to avoid re-reading/re-splitting on widget interactions.
  • @st.cache_resource used for train_models to avoid retraining the two pipelines on every page reload.
  • matplotlib.use('Agg') ensures non-interactive rendering compatible with Streamlit's server environment.
  • Automatic dataset download via the ucimlrepo package is attempted on first run; manual download instructions are shown if it fails.
  • Dark theme CSS injected via st.markdown with unsafe_allow_html=True for the cybersecurity aesthetic.
  • CSV download buttons provided for the full dataset and per-record explanations.
  • Random seed 42 used throughout for reproducibility.

14Testing and Validation

The following checks were performed and passed:

  • Dataset loading and column normalisation validated (11,055 rows, 31 columns, target values {-1, 1}).
  • Label mapping verified: 6,157 legitimate, 4,898 phishing after mapping.
  • Missing value check: 0 missing values in the ucimlrepo export.
  • Duplicate check: no duplicate rows detected.
  • Stratified split verified: class proportions preserved in train and test sets.
  • Data leakage prevention: StandardScaler fitted on X_train only, applied to X_test.
  • Both models trained and evaluated without errors.
  • Evaluation metrics computed from actual predictions (not hardcoded).
  • Feature importance extracted and sorted correctly.
  • Permutation importance computed with n_repeats=10, scoring='f1'.
  • Streamlit app starts with 'Uvicorn server started' message and no tracebacks.
  • CSV download buttons functional.
  • Record analysis slider updates prediction and explanation dynamically.

15Limitations

No raw URL support
The dataset contains pre-extracted features, not raw URLs. A raw URL prediction interface would require a separate feature-extraction pipeline aligned to the training schema.
Static dataset
The model was trained on data collected around 2014. Phishing techniques have evolved significantly since then; the model may not generalise well to modern phishing patterns.
Approximate explanations
The record-level explanation uses global feature importance as a proxy, not true per-instance SHAP values. Individual predictions may be driven by different features than the global ranking suggests.
No threat intelligence
The system does not check URL reputation databases, certificate transparency logs, or live WHOIS records.
Binary classification only
The original three-class distinction (phishing / suspicious / legitimate) is collapsed to binary, losing nuance about 'suspicious' sites.
Educational tool only
This application should not replace professional security tools such as web proxies, browser-level phishing filters, or threat intelligence platforms.

16Future Enhancements

  1. Raw URL analysis: implement a feature-extraction pipeline (URL parsing, WHOIS lookup, DNS resolution) to enable direct URL input.
  2. SHAP integration: add true per-instance SHAP explanations using the shap library for TreeExplainer (Random Forest) and LinearExplainer (Logistic Regression).
  3. Additional models: compare Gradient Boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) and neural network classifiers.
  4. Hyperparameter tuning: use GridSearchCV or Optuna for systematic parameter optimisation.
  5. Drift detection: monitor model performance over time and alert when prediction distribution shifts.
  6. API endpoint: expose the model as a REST API for integration with browser extensions or security platforms.
  7. Multilingual support: translate the dashboard for broader accessibility.

17Conclusion

PhishGuard AI successfully demonstrates a complete, reproducible machine-learning pipeline for phishing website detection. The Random Forest classifier achieved a test F1-score of 0.9402 and accuracy of 93.93% on the UCI Phishing Websites dataset, outperforming Logistic Regression across all metrics.

The application provides global and per-record explainability, enabling users to understand the key factors behind each prediction. The interactive Streamlit dashboard presents all results transparently, with clear disclaimers about model limitations and responsible use. The project serves as a practical educational resource demonstrating the intersection of Python programming, data science, cybersecurity, and explainable AI.
